ta-l1d5q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 5, where Lombard asks whether abstract essential names, like 'divine essence', can stand to generation as its subject or terminus. Lombard argues that the Father did not beget the divine essence. If he had, the essence would be relative to the Father; the Father would beget what he himself is; and the Father would have being through what he begot. He also argues that the essence does not beget the essence or the Son. Thomas maps Lombard's handling of contrary texts from Augustine and Hilary and of the scriptural phrase that the Father begot the Son 'from his substance'. He announces three inquiries: whether the essence is related to generation as begetter, as that from which generation is, or as its terminus. The first has two articles: whether the essence begets, and whether the same holds for other essential names.
claims: The divine essence is neither the terminus nor the subject of generation.
If the Father begot the essence, he would beget what he himself is and have being through what he begot.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e140.summary: First objection that the essence begets. Contradiction is a greater opposition than relation, and relative opposition makes one person not another. So contradiction would do so all the more. The Father is begetting, so if the essence does not beget, the Father is not the essence, which is impossible.
claims: Contradictory opposition is greater than relative opposition.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e143.summary: Second objection. Whatever is predicated of something can supposit for it. The essence is truly predicated of the Father, so it can supposit for him and take his predicates, including begetting.
claims: What is predicated of something can supposit for it.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e146.summary: Third objection. If the essence is the Father, it is the Father of the Son. Relatives convert, so the Son is the Son of the essence and the essence begets.
claims: Relative terms are convertible.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e150.summary: Fourth objection. The essence is the begetting thing (res generans), and the begetting thing begets, so the essence begets.
claims: The essence is the begetting reality.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e153.summary: Fifth objection. Essence relates to person as person to essence. Essential attributes such as power and goodness are predicated of a person, so personal properties can be predicated of the essence, and the essence begets.
claims: Essence and person stand symmetrically to each other in predication.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e156.summary: Notes that the contrary is shown by Lombard's arguments.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e159.summary: Thomas's determination. In creatures, acts belong to supposits: the essence does not act but is the principle of action in the supposit, so humanity does not beget but Socrates does by the power of his nature. Since essence differs really from supposit in creatures, no act is properly predicated of the essence except causally. In God essence and supposit do not differ really, only conceptually or in mode of signifying, the supposit as distinct and the essence as common. So whatever is predicated of the supposit not in the respect in which it differs from the essence is also predicated of the essence: the essence creates and governs. But an act predicated of the supposit in the respect in which it differs from the essence cannot be predicated of the essence. Begetting is such an act, said of the Father as distinct from the Son. So the essence does not beget; the Father begets by the power of the essence or nature (Damascene: generation is a work of the divine nature).
claims: In God, acts said of a person as distinct from the essence cannot be predicated of the essence.
The essence creates and governs, but does not beget; the Father begets by the power of the nature.
Acts belong to supposits, the nature being their principle.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the first objection. Affirmation and negation are most opposed because they imply no agreement. Privative opposites agree in subject, and contrary and relative opposites also in genus, so both extremes are signified as beings and natures. What is found unmixed with its contrary is first in a genus and cause of the rest, so contradiction is the first and greatest opposition and is included in every other as the prior in the posterior. Other oppositions require more, by addition. So even if contrariety requires real diversity, affirmation and negation do not; conceptual distinction suffices, and that is what lies between essence and person. Relative opposites sometimes require real distinction (as between the divine persons) and sometimes only conceptual distinction (as in 'the same is the same as itself'), a point treated more fully in Dist. 26.
claims: Contradiction is the first and greatest opposition and is included in all others.
A conceptual distinction suffices for affirmation and negation, as between essence and person.
Relative opposition sometimes requires real and sometimes only conceptual distinction.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e165.summary: Reply to the second objection. The essence is predicated of the supposit not because of the mode of signifying of both but because of their real indifference, owing to the simplicity of the divine nature. So it need not supposit for the Father.
claims: The essence is predicated of the persons because of real identity, not shared mode of signifying.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the third objection. 'The essence is the Father' is ambiguous. If 'Father' is taken adjectivally, placing its form on the essence, it is false, since properties do not determine the essence. If taken substantively, suppositing for the Father's person, it is true, but the conversion yields not 'the Son is the Son of the essence' but 'the Son is the Son of the Father, who is the essence'.
claims: 'The essence is the Father' is true only with 'Father' taken substantively.
Personal properties do not determine the essence.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. In 'the essence is the begetting thing', 'thing' can supposit for the essence, in which case the proposition is false because the adjective would place its form on the essence, or for the person, in which case it is true. But then it does not follow that the essence is begetting, since the adjective's form does not bear on the same thing.
claims: 'Res generans' is true of the essence only if 'res' stands for the person, which blocks the inference.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Since essence and person differ in mode of signifying, what is predicated of a person by the mode in which it is distinguished from the essence (begetting, begotten) is not predicated of the essence. Conversely, what is predicated of the essence by the mode in which it differs from a distinct supposit is not predicated of a person: the essence is common to the three, but this cannot be said of any person.
claims: Predicates belonging to a person as distinct, or to the essence as common, do not transfer across.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e187.summary: First objection that begetting is predicated of no essential name. The three persons are one essence and also one God. If 'the essence begets' is denied lest it imply distinction in the essence, 'God begets' should be denied lest it imply several gods.
claims: 'God begets' would imply several gods as 'the essence begets' implies distinct essences.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e190.summary: Second objection. Person, hypostasis, and substance are not said relatively, and according to Lombard the essence cannot beget because it is not said relatively. So neither can person or hypostasis.
claims: Lombard denies begetting to the essence because it is not relative.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e193.summary: Third objection. Nature, goodness, and the like are as abstract as essence. If the essence cannot beget because of its abstract mode of signifying, neither can they.
claims: Nature and goodness are as abstract as essence.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e197.summary: Notes that the contrary is shown by many authorities cited in Lombard's text.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e200.summary: Thomas's determination. Begetting properly belongs to a supposit as distinct, so the closer a name comes to signifying a distinct supposit, the more truly begetting is predicated of it. 'The Father begets' is most proper, since 'Father' is imposed from a distinguishing property. 'A person begets' is also fitting, since 'person' is imposed from the common property of personality. 'God begets' is less proper, since 'God' includes a supposit but not a distinct one and is imposed from the common essence. Among abstract names there is also an order. Some imply ordering to act (power, goodness, light, nature), so since acts are of supposits, phrases like 'wisdom begets' or 'nature begets' are found; they are not to be extended but understood piously. Others are imposed from the act of standing under, like 'substance', which still approaches the notion of supposit. 'Essence' is wholly removed from the notion of supposit, so 'the essence begets' is least admissible and, if found, must be read as 'the Father, who is the essence, begets'.
claims: Begetting is predicated more properly the closer a name comes to a distinct supposit: Father, then person, then God.
Abstract names ordered to act, such as nature and wisdom, can be said to beget only in a pious, non-extendable sense.
'Essence' is most removed from the supposit, so 'the essence begets' is least admissible.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first objection. 'God' includes a supposit indeterminately and, by what it is imposed from, includes the nature. By mode of signifying it is a kind of mean between essence and distinct person. It is compatible both with the essence's mode, given its indeterminacy, and with the distinct person's, given its supposit. So one can say both 'God begets' and 'God is common to the three persons'.
claims: 'Deus' is a mean between essence and distinct person in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second objection, distinguishing senses of 'relative' in divine names. Most properly, it is a name referred to another by its very name (Father). Next, a name that follows on or causes relation (generation, to beget). Next, one that implicitly includes relation (Trinity, which includes persons distinguished by relation, and 'person', which includes the distinguishing relation). Finally, one that stands for a relation, like 'God' and certain abstract names, for the reason given.
claims: Divine names can be relative by signification, by causing relation, by implicit inclusion, or by standing for a relation.

ta-l1d5q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the third objection. 'Essence' is more abstract than 'goodness' or 'wisdom'. They abstract equally from the supposit, but 'essence' also abstracts from act, whereas the others imply ordering to act.
claims: 'Essence' abstracts from act as well as from supposit, unlike goodness and wisdom.

ta-l1d5q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 5 maps Lombard's arguments that the divine essence is neither the terminus nor the subject of generation, and his responses to contrary authorities from Augustine and Hilary. It announces inquiries into the essence as begetter, as that from which, and as terminus of generation.
claims: The divine essence neither begets nor is begotten.

ta-l1d5q1-Dd1e132.summary: Article 1 asks whether the essence begets. Objections argue from the strength of contradictory opposition, from predication and supposition, from the convertibility of relatives, from 'res generans', and from the symmetry of essence and person. Thomas holds that acts belong to supposits, with the nature as their principle. Since in God essence and person differ only in mode of signifying, acts said of a person without reference to its distinction (creating, governing) are also said of the essence. Acts said of a person as distinct, such as begetting, are not: the Father begets by the power of the nature. The replies give a theory of opposition, on which contradiction is the first opposition and needs only conceptual distinction. They resolve the convertibility and 'res generans' arguments by adjectival and substantival construals and block the transfer of distinctive personal and essential predicates.
claims: The essence does not beget; the Father begets by the power of the divine nature.
Essential acts like creating are said of the essence; notional acts like begetting are not.
Contradiction requires only conceptual distinction.

ta-l1d5q1-Dd1e179.summary: Article 2 asks whether begetting can be predicated of other essential names. Thomas ranks names by proximity to a distinct supposit: 'Father' (most proper), 'person', 'God', abstract names ordered to act such as nature and wisdom (admissible only in a pious, non-extendable sense), 'substance', and finally 'essence', which is wholly removed from supposit and least of all can be said to beget. The replies treat 'God' as a mean between essence and person, distinguish four senses of 'relative' in divine names, and note that 'essence' is the most abstract name because it abstracts from act as well as from supposit.
claims: Begetting is predicated more or less properly of divine names according to their proximity to a distinct supposit.
'Essence' is the most abstract divine name and the least able to take notional predicates.

ta-l1d5q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 5 asks whether the divine essence is related to generation as begetter. Article 1 denies that the essence begets. Acts belong to supposits, with the nature as their principle, and since essence and person differ in God only in mode of signifying, essential acts (creating, governing) may be said of the essence while notional acts (begetting), said of a person as distinct, may not. The Father begets by the power of the nature. Article 2 ranks divine names by proximity to a distinct supposit, from 'Father' through 'person', 'God', 'nature', and 'substance' to 'essence', which is the most abstract and the least able to bear notional predicates. Along the way Thomas gives a theory of opposition, on which contradiction requires only conceptual distinction, and a typology of relative names.
claims: The divine essence does not beget; the Father begets by the power of the nature.
Notional acts are predicated of divine names in proportion to their proximity to a distinct supposit.
Essential acts may be predicated of the essence; notional acts may not.
